\chapter{Five More Things You Ask For --- Rope, Needle, Thread, Basket, Paper}
\label{ch:mas-cosas-que-pedir}
\hlchaptermodality{301}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask for a rope, a needle, thread, a basket and paper in Spanish, politely.}

Complete ES-C301-papel: ask for all five in turn, with por favor on the end of each.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[la cuerda]{la cuerda — a string made of gut}

\label{lesson:ES-C301-cuerda}



\begin{quote}
Before a new run: what does \emph{sangfroid} mean, taken literally? (Cold blood.) And what does \emph{no hay remedio} say? (There is nothing to be done.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item por favor — what goes on the end of every ask in this run.
  \item el puente — a thing that has been made out of these.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{CUER-da}, stress on the first part. The \emph{ue} is one slide and the \emph{d} is soft. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la cuerda} — \textquotedblleft{}the rope,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}the cord,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}the string.\textquotedblright{}

Greek \textbf{khordē} meant a gut — an intestine — and then the string made out of one, because that is what strings were made of. Latin borrowed it as \textbf{chorda}, and the stressed \emph{o} did what it always does under stress in Spanish: it cracked open into \emph{ue}. So \emph{chorda} became \emph{cuerda}, by the same road as \emph{somnus} to \emph{sueño}.

English kept the gut in a whole shelf of words. A \textbf{cord} is the plain rope. A \textbf{chord} is what several strings sound together. A \textbf{cordon} is a rope drawn round a place to keep people out. And a \textbf{harpsichord} is, quite literally, a harp made of gut strings.

So this is not a rough word for a rough object. It is a musical instrument's word that ended up in the shed.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five things to ask for, and the \emph{ue} crack has now paid twice in two runs.

\emph{Sueño} and \emph{cuerda} are the same event happening to two unrelated words. That is what makes it a rule rather than a coincidence.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la cuerda}
  \item \emph{la cuerda, por favor}
  \item \emph{el sueño}, then \emph{la cuerda} — the same crack twice
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{khordē} mean first? (A gut, then a string made of one.) Which English instrument is a gut-stringed harp? (A harpsichord.) And what did the stressed \emph{o} do? (Broke into \emph{ue}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la aguja]{la aguja — the sharp you already write}

\label{lesson:ES-C301-aguja}



\begin{quote}
Two back: what does \emph{no hay remedio} say? (There is nothing to be done.) And what did \emph{khordē} mean? (A gut, then a string made from one.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la cuerda — the thick one, from just before.
  \item la oveja — the word this one rhymes with, and for the same reason.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{a-GU-ja}, stress in the middle. The \emph{gu} is a hard \emph{g}, and the \emph{j} is the scrape. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la aguja} — \textquotedblleft{}the needle.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{acus} was a needle, and behind it lay a much older idea: sharpness. Add the small-and-fond ending and you get \textbf{acucula}, a little sharp thing — which came down to Spanish as \emph{aguja}, by the very road that turned \emph{ovicula} into \emph{oveja}. That is why the two words rhyme.

Now the useful part. That \emph{acus} is standing in the corner of every page you have read. The accent you write on \emph{sartén} is called \textbf{acute}, and \emph{acute} is just Latin for sharp — a sharp accent, as against the grave one that leans the other way. You have been writing the same root for a long time without being told.

The rest of the family is easy once you have it. \textbf{Acupuncture} is puncturing with sharps. \textbf{Acumen} is a sharp mind. \textbf{Acid} is a sharp taste. All of them are this needle.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two of the five, and a root you were already using in silence.

\emph{La cuerda} and \emph{la aguja} also belong together in the hand: the thick one and the one that pulls the thin one through.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la aguja}
  \item \emph{la aguja, por favor}
  \item \emph{la oveja}, then \emph{la aguja} — the same ending, twice
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{acus} mean? (A needle — a sharp.) Why is the acute accent called that? (\emph{Acute} is Latin for sharp.) And which word does \emph{aguja} rhyme with, and why? (\emph{Oveja} — both came from the same small ending.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el hilo]{el hilo — the second h with an f under it}

\label{lesson:ES-C301-hilo}



\begin{quote}
What did \emph{khordē} mean? (A gut, then a string.) And why is the acute accent called acute? (Because \emph{acute} is Latin for sharp.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el horno — the first word this run gave you with a buried \emph{f}.
  \item la aguja — what pulls this through the cloth.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{I-lo}, two beats, and the \emph{h} is silent. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el hilo} — \textquotedblleft{}the thread.\textquotedblright{}

Run the decoder. Silent \emph{h} at the front: put an \emph{f} back and see what falls out. \textbf{Filum} — Latin for a thread. It works, and it works for the same reason it worked on \emph{horno}.

English took \emph{filum} the bookish way and kept every letter. A \textbf{filament} is a fine thread in a lamp. \textbf{Filigree} is metal worked into threads. A \textbf{profile} is a line drawn round something. And soldiers walking in \textbf{single file} are walking in one thread, which is a much older picture than the parade ground.

There is also a phrase worth carrying: \emph{perder el hilo}, to lose the thread — of an argument, of a conversation. English says exactly the same thing about exactly the same object, and neither borrowed it. Everybody who has ever talked too long has felt the thread go.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three of the five, and the \emph{f}-to-\emph{h} decoder has now paid twice.

\emph{Horno} and \emph{hilo} are both Latin words with a letter worn off the front. When you meet the next silent \emph{h}, try the same trick before you look anything up.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el hilo}
  \item \emph{el hilo, por favor}
  \item \emph{la aguja y el hilo}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was \emph{filum}? (A thread.) What is a \emph{filament}? (A fine thread.) And what does \emph{perder el hilo} mean? (To lose the thread of something.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la cesta]{la cesta — one box, two English words}

\label{lesson:ES-C301-cesta}



\begin{quote}
Three questions. What was \emph{chorda}? (A gut string.) What was \emph{acus}? (A needle.) And what was \emph{filum}? (A thread.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la manzana — what people carry in one.
  \item el hilo — the thing before this one.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{CES-ta}, stress on the first part. The \emph{c} before \emph{e} is the soft one. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la cesta} — \textquotedblleft{}the basket.\textquotedblright{}

Greek \textbf{kistē} was a box. Latin took it as \textbf{cista}, and Spanish wore it down to \emph{cesta}, keeping the shape and losing nothing important.

English got the same box twice, by two different doors, and the pair is a good demonstration of what those doors do. Through Germanic mouths, early and worn: a \textbf{chest}, which is a box you can sit on. Straight out of the books, late and tidy: a \textbf{cistern}, which is a tank for water and still sounds like an engineer's word.

That is the general pattern, and once you have seen it here you will see it everywhere. Words that came the long way, through everyday speech, sound plain. Words that came the short way, through writing, sound learned. Same origin, different mileage.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four of the five, and a rule about English that keeps explaining Spanish.

When a Spanish word looks like a plain English word and a fancy one at once, that is usually not a coincidence. It is one Latin word that took two routes.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la cesta}
  \item \emph{la cesta, por favor}
  \item all four — \emph{la cuerda}, \emph{la aguja}, \emph{el hilo}, \emph{la cesta}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was \emph{cista}? (A box.) Which English word for it came the worn, everyday way? (\emph{Chest}.) And which came straight out of the books? (\emph{Cistern}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el papel]{el papel — a reed, and a part in a play}

\label{lesson:ES-C301-papel}



\begin{quote}
Before the last of the five: what was \emph{acus}? (A needle.) What was \emph{filum}? (A thread.) And which English word is \emph{cista}, worn down? (\emph{Chest}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el libro — named after what people wrote on before this arrived.
  \item escribir — what you do on it.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pa-PEL}, stress on the end, and no accent needed for a word ending in \emph{-l}. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el papel} — \textquotedblleft{}the paper.\textquotedblright{}

Behind it is \textbf{papyrus}, the Egyptian reed whose pith was beaten flat and written on for three thousand years. English \textbf{paper} is the same reed. So is the \textbf{papyrus} in a museum case, which is the word arriving a second time, unworn, to name the original thing.

Put that beside \emph{el libro}. A \emph{libro} is named after the inner bark of a tree, which is what people wrote on when there was no papyrus to hand. Two writing surfaces, two words, and neither of them has anything to do with writing — both are named after a plant.

Then \emph{papel} did something Latin never asked it to. It also means the \textbf{part} an actor plays, because the part used to be handed to the actor written out on a sheet. \emph{Hacer el papel de} — to play the part of. English keeps the same idea in \textbf{role}, which was a little roll of paper.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five: \emph{la cuerda}, \emph{la aguja}, \emph{el hilo}, \emph{la cesta}, \emph{el papel}.

Ask for any of them with \emph{por favor} on the end and you have a complete, polite request — the same shape you have been using since the soap and the towel.

And every one of the five is named after a material rather than a use: a gut, a sharp, a thread, a box, a reed. Objects get their names from what they are made of far more often than from what they are for, which is the opposite of the rule the farm gave you. Both are true; that is why you need to have met both.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el papel}
  \item \emph{el papel, por favor}
  \item all five with \emph{por favor} — \emph{la cuerda}, \emph{la aguja}, \emph{el hilo}, \emph{la cesta}, \emph{el papel}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What plant is \emph{papel} named after? (The papyrus reed.) What is \emph{el libro} named after? (The inner bark of a tree.) And what else does \emph{papel} mean? (The part an actor plays.)
\end{tcolorbox}
